transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-25 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Ethan Diaz (Redwood EngOps), Jill Ramos (CacheCraft CTO), Marcus Lee (ML Eng), Sofia Nguyen (Infra), Tom Brooks (PM)
Shared files: https://redwood.app/shared/benchmarks/cachecraft-poc-2026-02-20.xlsx, https://redwood.app/docs/continuous-batching-overview.pdf

Summary (auto - may be rough):
- Reviewed last week's benchmark where sustained throughput improved with continuous batching but p95 tail latency increased under bursty traffic.
- Agreed to test narrower concurrency caps and request-level queueing; run an additional sweep for batch size + concurrency combos.
- Next steps to exchange traces and set SLOs for tail latency and throughput.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): ok everybody welcome back, thanks for making time. quick roll call?
[00:05] Jill (CacheCraft - CTO): yeah hi thanks, Jill here. Marcus, Sofia and Tom from our side.
[00:09] Marcus (CacheCraft - ML Eng): yep I'm here.
[00:10] Ravi (Redwood SE): Ravi here, I'll lead the perf bits today. Ethan's taking notes.
[00:13] Maya: cool, agenda - 1) run review, 2) what we tuned, 3) planned sweep, 4) next steps.
[00:18] Jill: sounds good. we've been watching the dashboard. we saw throughput up but p95 spiked which worries product.
[00:24] Ravi: yeah that's what we want to dig into. quick recap: last run used continuous batching with max batch 32 and concurrency 12 on the dedicated instance. average tokens/sec went from ~6k -> ~14k per GPU, sustained. but we saw p95 go from 180ms to ~420ms under bursty windows.
[00:42] Marcus: correct; the bursts are from our web tier during peak. request sizes vary a lot, some short chat prompts, some long completion jobs. the distribution is skewed, long tail.
[00:54] Ravi: right, so continuous batching reduces per-token cost by filling batches but can increase queueing time for small low-latency requests. two levers: lower max batch size or introduce concurrency caps + per-request queue timeout, or use hybrid - immediate-fast path for small requests.
[01:15] Sofia (CacheCraft - Infra): what's the immediate-fast path look like? like serve small requests on separate pool?
[01:20] Ravi: could be. options: 1) route <128 token requests to a low-latency pool with small batch cap, 2) use concurrency cap and queueing to prioritize low-latency, 3) enable prefix/KV cache to reduce compute for repeated prompts. each has tradeoffs on cost.
[01:36] Jill: cost is a factor; we want to keep unit cost low but can't have customer-facing latency spikes.
[01:40] Maya: agreed; our recommendation this week was run A,B,C sweep - change concurrency 8/12/16 and batch caps 16/32/48 and enable a short queue TTL of 50/150/300ms. we ran three configs already and shared the sheet.
[01:54] Tom (CacheCraft - PM): can you summarize which config looked best?
[01:58] Ravi: sure - config B (concurrency 12, batch 32, queue TTL 150ms) had best throughput-cost tradeoff but p95 during surge windows hit ~420ms. config A (concurrency 8, batch 16) lowered p95 to ~220ms but throughput dropped ~30% so cost per token went up. config C (concurrency 16, batch 48) improved throughput marginally but p99 tail worsened due to queue stacking.
[02:22] Marcus: do we have histograms? the spreadsheet has them - link above - but maybe show quick numbers live?
[02:28] Ethan (Redwood): I pasted the key table in the chat: avg latency, p50, p95, p99, tokens/sec, effective tokens/second/gpu.
[02:35] Jill: i see it... config A p95 220ms p99 640ms tokens/sec 9.8k. config B p95 420ms p99 980ms tokens/sec 13.7k. config C p95 580ms p99 1.4s tokens/sec 14.5k.
[02:52] Maya: so high level: continuous batching achieved the token throughput we wanted but increased tail latency under burst load. we need to tune queueing and priority to protect small requests.
[03:02] Sofia: question - can we do per-route QoS? like certain endpoints prioritized?
[03:07] Ravi: yes; Redwood supports route-level priority and capacity reservations. you can reserve a small percentage of the pool for low-latency routes (eg 15-20%). that reduces throughput available for big jobs but gives consistent latency.
[03:18] Marcus: what's the effort to add a low-latency reserve vs just tuning concurrency?
[03:22] Ravi: reserve is config change on our side, minimal. the big effort is deciding which endpoints to classify. tuning concurrency is faster but less guaranteed isolation.
[03:32] Jill: we like reservation because it maps to business SLAs. can we simulate a 20% reserve?
[03:36] Ravi: yes we can run a sim. we should also test hybrid: reserve 20% + continuous batching on remaining 80% with a slightly higher batch cap. that often hits both throughput and tail targets.
[03:46] Tom: and queue TTLs, you mentioned 50/150/300ms - what's the user impact?
[03:50] Ravi: shorter TTL means less queuing so lower latency but smaller batch sizes -> higher cost. TTL 150ms was our middle ground; 50ms keeps p95 lower but tokens/sec drops. 300ms gives max throughput but hurts small requests.
[04:04] Marcus: any model-level knobs? quantization?
[04:06] Maya: we recommended the fp16 q4_0 quantized variant for this POC to save memory; but quantization vs latency tradeoffs were minor compared to batching/queueing.
[04:15] Jill: on KV cache - would that help both cost and latency?
[04:18] Ravi: yes for repeated prefixes. if many requests share initial context, KV caching avoids recompute and reduces tokens processed, improving both throughput and latency for cached hits. we need sample traffic to estimate hit rate.
[04:28] Marcus: we'll share the real production trace ASAP. question: what's our SLA target? we've been throwing numbers but product needs a concrete SLO.
[04:36] Tom: we were thinking 200ms p95 for customer-facing chat, and 800ms for background generation.
[04:42] Maya: that's reasonable. config A got close but cost was high. I think hybrid reserve with concurrency cap is the right next experiment to aim for 200ms p95 while keeping tokens/sec >=12k.
[04:53] Jill: ok let's try that.
[04:55] Ravi: proposed plan for next run: 1) reserve 20% capacity for low-latency route, 2) apply continuous batching on remaining 80% with max batch 32, concurrency 12, queue TTL 150ms, 3) run for a 2-hour soak with synthetic burst overlay matching customer trace. we'll capture p50/p95/p99 and throughput and cost estimates.
[05:16] Marcus: how soon can you run it?
[05:18] Ravi: we can run tomorrow if we get the traces today, otherwise Friday. run will take ~3 hours including warmup and artifact collection.
[05:25] Jill: we'll upload traces by EOD Thursday.
[05:28] Maya: next steps recap - Redwood runs the reserved/hybrid config and share detailed histograms + cost delta, CacheCraft provides traces + confirms which routes to reserve, Redwood to send updated pricing.
[05:38] Tom: also please add timezone notes - we need the run during our peak window which is 17:00 - 19:00 UTC.
[05:43] Ethan: noted. we'll schedule soak for peak window after we get traces.
[05:47] Jill: one more question - security/compliance: any extra requirements for the soak run? we prefer no real PII in traces.
[05:53] Maya: absolutely, scrubbed traces only. we'll use synthetic load that mirrors distributions. and we can run inside your VPC for private if needed later.
[06:01] Marcus: ok will scrub and share.
[06:04] Ravi: action items captured in chat. any other blockers?
[06:07] Jill: none from my side. thanks team.
[06:10] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the run results and updated cost table. 
[06:14] end of call

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-attributions and filler words; speaker-turn overlaps.

Artifacts to be delivered: run results CSV/Excel + histograms, updated pricing, recommended routing config JSON (sent as text in email).
